knownFor: Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine who set out to write the church's story from its own letters and lists, wrote the emperor Constantine's Life, and was charged at Tyre with having got out of prison by giving way.
shortDescription: Eusebius was bishop of Caesarea in Roman Palestine. He believed he was the first to try to tell the church's story from Christ to his own day, and he built it from the letters, lists and books of the Christians before him. He lived through the emperors' persecution of the church and wrote the emperor Constantine's Life. At Tyre a bishop who had suffered in the persecution charged that he had got out of prison by giving way.
datesNote: No old source used here gives the year he was born or the year he became bishop. He dates the first orders of the persecution to the nineteenth year of Diocletian, which is 303, and writes that he saw it. His own letter shows him a priest and then a bishop by the council of Nicaea in 325. Epiphanius places him at Tyre in 335. He died after Constantine, in the reign of Constantine's sons, Socrates says. Modern reckonings of his birth and death are in the works listed under Modern works.
placeNote: Caesarea, on the coast of Roman Palestine, where he was bishop; Nicaea in Bithynia, where the council met in 325; Tyre, the chief city of Phoenicia, where the bishops met in 335

keyWorks.title: Church History
keyWorks.about: the church from Christ to his own day, built from the documents he could find

keyWorks.title: Life of Constantine
keyWorks.about: a book on the emperor's faith, written after his death, which by its own rule leaves out his wars and laws

traces: Socrates of Constantinople began his own history of the church with what Eusebius had left out, after the point where Eusebius closed his History: the end of the persecution under Constantine.

Theodoret of Cyrrhus says he will begin his history from the period at which Eusebius's ends. Sozomen counts Eusebius among the writers who had set down the church's past before him, and writes on from where they ended. Evagrius Scholasticus, in the late sixth century, names Eusebius first among four earlier church historians in the preface to his own.

Rufinus of Aquileia put the Church History into Latin, at the request of Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, when the Goths broke into Italy, and wrote two books more. Jerome says the History was of the utmost assistance to his own book on Christian writers, and he carried Eusebius's Chronicle, a table of events by year, on in Latin from the twentieth year of Constantine.

Eusebius copies earlier writers' letters whole into his History. The letter of Polycrates of Ephesus to Victor and the church of Rome on the day for keeping Easter stands in it in full. He quotes Josephus on Jesus, and he retells, from the Latin Apology of Tertullian, Pliny the Younger's letter to the emperor Trajan about the Christians and Trajan's reply.

Eusebius says he was present at Tyre when martyrs were thrown to wild beasts, and on the spot in the Thebais, in upper Egypt, where he saw large crowds in one day, some beheaded and others tortured by fire.
Acacius, his disciple, followed him as bishop of Caesarea and published a life of his master, Socrates says.
remembered: Sabinus, a bishop of Heraclea in Thrace, scorned the Council of Nicaea but still called Eusebius a trustworthy witness, Socrates of Constantinople says.
Jerome, in his Letter 84, says Eusebius composed a fine history of the Church.

uncertain: At Tyre in 335 Potamo, a bishop from Heraclea in Egypt and a confessor, which is a Christian who suffered for the faith in the persecution and lived, asked Eusebius how he had got out of prison unless he had promised or done what was forbidden. Only Epiphanius of Salamis tells it. He wrote about forty years later, on the side of Athanasius of Alexandria, and calls the charges against Athanasius slanders. No work of Eusebius used here says he was jailed, and no old source used here says he gave way, or that he was cleared.

The bishops of Egypt, in a letter Athanasius kept in his Defence Against the Arians, ask whether Eusebius was not accused by their confessors over a sacrifice, an offering to the Roman gods of the kind the persecuting orders forced on church leaders. The Greek says only over a sacrifice; the words to idols are the English translator's. The letter is on Athanasius's side.

How he came to sign at Nicaea is told three ways. His own letter to his church says that he and the others agreed after questions about what the added word meant, for the sake of peace and so as not to fall from the right belief. The word is homoousios, which says the Son is of the same substance as the Father. Socrates of Constantinople, about a century later, says he held back for a short time before he signed, and sent his people the creed, the church's short statement of belief, so that no one would doubt his motives. Athanasius of Alexandria, who was at the council and was his opponent, says he had refused the day before.

How far he truly accepted the wording of the Nicene creed, with its added word, is argued. His own letter says he accepted it only after asking what it meant. Eustathius, bishop of Antioch, accused him of twisting it, Socrates says, and Eusebius denied it and answered with a charge of his own against Eustathius. After Eustathius was deposed, Socrates says, one party at Antioch wanted Eusebius moved there from Caesarea, and he refused.
Constantine's vision of a cross of light in the sky rests on what the emperor told Eusebius long afterwards, confirming it by an oath, as Eusebius says in the Life of Constantine.

Eusebius wrote that he was the first to enter on the subject of a church history and knew of no church writer who had given himself to it. Sozomen, about a century later, names Clement, Hegesippus and Africanus, as well as Eusebius, among the writers who had set down the church's past before him.

The month the persecution began is told three ways. Eusebius puts the edict ordering the churches torn down in March, in the nineteenth year of Diocletian, and his Martyrs of Palestine gives April. McGiffert's note reports that Lactantius, who was at Nicomedia, gives February 23. The year, 303, is not disputed.
No old source used here gives the year he was born or the year he became bishop.

Whether he presided at Tyre is not said by any old source used here. Epiphanius says the emperor ordered him to judge there, with some others, who he says leaned toward the Arians, the followers of Arius, who taught that God's Son had a beginning. Sozomen says Athanasius had earlier refused to attend a council at Caesarea, fearing the artifices of Eusebius, bishop of that city, and of Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia. Modern historians differ on who presided; Hefele's history of the councils, listed under Modern works, treats the question.

Rufinus of Aquileia, writing later in Latin, tells a like scene at Tyre that does not name Eusebius. In it Paphnutius, a confessor who had lost an eye, tells Maximus, bishop of Jerusalem, who had also been a confessor, with an eye put out and a leg hamstrung, that he will not let him sit in the council of the wicked.

Socrates says the charge that Athanasius's side had cut off a man's hand failed at Tyre when the man, Arsenius, was brought in alive with both hands. He says the council nevertheless voted to depose Athanasius as bishop, on the report of a one-sided inquiry at Mareotis, by Alexandria, and that its sentence said nothing of the failed charge. Eusebius's own part in the vote is not given.

In his Life of Constantine he says he will pass over the emperor's wars and laws and speak only of what bears on his religious character. Socrates says the book is more intent on the emperor's praise than on an accurate account. Its telling of the council at Tyre names neither Athanasius nor Potamo and says only that envy troubled the churches of Egypt.

Whether he held that the Son was less than the Father is judged both ways. Athanasius says that in a letter to Euphration, Eusebius said plainly that Christ was not true God. Socrates answers that Eusebius was at Nicaea and agreed to what it decided. Philostorgius, whom Photius's summary preserves, praises him but accuses him of erroneous opinions in matters of religion. Jerome calls him the most open champion of the Arian impiety in one letter and the standard-bearer of the Arian side in another work. In 787 the Second Council of Nicaea, answering those who used his letter to Constantia against holy images, read his letter to Euphration.

briefReferences: Church History I.1.1 to 6, tr. Arthur McGiffert: his plan, his claim to be the first, the brief fragments of those before him, the passages he gathered.
Church History VI.20.1, I.13.5 and V.24.1 to 2: the letters kept in the library at Aelia, the letters from the archives at Edessa, and Polycrates's letter to Victor copied whole.

Church History VIII.2.1 to 5: the churches thrown down, the Scriptures burned, the shepherds hiding; his rule to leave out those shaken by the persecution; the first edict in the nineteenth year of Diocletian; the second orders, jail and forced sacrifice. VIII.7.2 and VIII.9.4: what he saw at Tyre and in the Thebais.

Martyrs of Palestine 7 and 11: Pamphilus, his dearest friend, cast into prison, and his martyrdom with his companions. Church History VII.32.25: Pamphilus, a priest of the church at Caesarea. Church History VI.33.4: the Defense of Origen written with Pamphilus.
Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 81: the surname Pamphili from his friendship with Pamphilus.
Arius's letter to Eusebius of Nicomedia, in Theodoret I.4: Eusebius of Caesarea named among the bishops of the East Arius says were condemned.

His letter to his church on the Council of Nicaea, in McGiffert's Prolegomena, in Athanasius and in Socrates I.8: his church's creed read, the added word, the questions asked, assent not without inquiry, and peace as the aim.
Socrates I.8: he held aloof for a short time, then signed. Athanasius, Defence of the Nicene Definition 3: he had denied the day before, then signed.
Socrates I.23 and I.24, and Constantine's letter in Life of Constantine III.61: Eustathius's charge and Eusebius's answer; the refusal of Antioch.

Life of Constantine I.11, I.19, I.28, IV.33, IV.41 and IV.45: his rule to speak only of the emperor's religious character; Constantine seen as a young man; what the emperor told him himself under oath; the discourse the emperor stood to hear; the council at Tyre told without naming Athanasius or Potamo; the orations at the dedication in Jerusalem.

Sozomen II.25: Athanasius's refusal to attend a council at Caesarea. Epiphanius, Panarion 68.7 and 68.8, with Petavius's Latin and McGiffert's English: the charges against Athanasius, the council at Tyre, Potamo's words, Eusebius rises in anger and breaks up the court.
Socrates I.29 to 32: the charge of the hand, the inquiry at Mareotis, the vote to depose Athanasius.
Athanasius, Defence Against the Arians, letter of the council of Egypt: the charge that Eusebius was accused over a sacrifice, with the Greek in Migne.
Rufinus, Church History X.18: a like scene at Tyre, with no word of Eusebius. Rufinus, prologue: the Church History put into Latin.

Socrates I.1: his history begins where Eusebius stopped; the Life of Constantine more intent on the emperor's praise than on an accurate account. Theodoret I.1, Sozomen I.1 and the preface of Evagrius: histories that begin after him.
Jerome, Chronicle at Constantine's twentieth year, and Lives of Illustrious Men, preface: his Chronicle carried on, and the utmost assistance of his History.

Socrates I.8 and II.21, Athanasius On the Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia 17, the Epitome of Philostorgius I.2, Jerome Letter 84 and Apology I, and the acts of the Second Council of Nicaea: how he was judged.
Church History V.24, I.11 and III.33: Polycrates of Ephesus's letter on Easter, the passage on Jesus in Josephus, and Pliny the Younger's letter to Trajan, taken from Tertullian.
Socrates II.4: Acacius, his pupil, who followed him as bishop and wrote his life.

quotationOriginals.modern: I admit that a perfect and complete history is beyond my power. I am the first to take up this subject, so I am trying to travel, as it were, a lonely and untrodden path.
quotationOriginals.printed: I confess that it is beyond my power to produce a perfect and complete history, and since I am the first to enter upon the subject, I am attempting to traverse as it were a lonely and untrodden path.
quotationOriginals.work: Church History I.1.4, tr. Arthur McGiffert
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The Greek of Books 1 to 5 is not held, so the wording rests on McGiffert's English. The modern wording gives confess as admit, its sense here, not a confession of wrong.

quotationOriginals.modern: We saw with our own eyes the houses of prayer thrown down from top to ground, foundations and all. We saw the inspired and holy Scriptures handed to the fire in the middle of the market squares. We saw the shepherds of the churches hiding shamefully here and there, and some of them caught in disgrace and mocked by their enemies.
quotationOriginals.printed: we saw with our own eyes the houses of prayer thrown down to the very foundations, and the Divine and Sacred Scriptures committed to the flames in the midst of the market-places, and the shepherds of the churches basely hidden here and there, and some of them captured ignominiously, and mocked by their enemies.
quotationOriginals.work: Church History VIII.2.1, tr. Arthur McGiffert
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The Greek is held only in a damaged scan of Schwartz's edition (lines 13614 to 13620 of the Greek and Latin Church History file), so the card prints McGiffert's English. The modern wording follows the Greek, checked by hand: from top to ground, foundations and all, is the Greek from a height to the ground, with the foundations themselves. The Greek has one verb, we saw, for all three sights; the modern wording says it once for each. Rufinus's Latin in the same file renders the passage freely.

quotationOriginals.modern: Tell me, were you not with me in prison in the persecution? I lost an eye for the truth. But you seem to have nothing maimed in your body. You did not suffer as a martyr. You stand alive, with nothing cut away. How did you get out of prison, unless you promised those who forced the persecution on us to do the forbidden thing, or did it?
quotationOriginals.printed: Pray tell me, wast thou not with me in prison during the persecution? And I lost an eye in behalf of the truth, but thou appearest to have received no bodily injury, neither hast thou suffered martyrdom, but thou hast remained alive with no mutilation. How wast thou released from prison unless thou didst promise those that put upon us the pressure of persecution to do that which is unlawful, or didst actually do it?
quotationOriginals.work: Epiphanius, Panarion 68.8, as Arthur McGiffert gives it in the Prolegomena
quotationOriginals.uncertain: These are the words Epiphanius gives Potamo, written about forty years later on Athanasius's side. The Greek is held only in a damaged scan (lines 44592 to 44604 of the Epiphanius file); the modern wording follows it, checked by hand, and agrees with Petavius's Latin in the same file (lines 44670 to 44675). Those who forced the persecution on us renders those who brought the compulsion of the persecution on us, and the forbidden thing renders the Greek that which is not permitted. The brief leaves out the question Who can bear such things? that stands before the first sentence.

timeline.headline: A friend of Pamphilus, and the plan of a History

lines.text: He becomes acquainted with Pamphilus, a priest of the church at Caesarea, whom he later calls his dearest friend.
lines.reference: Church History VII.32.25; Martyrs of Palestine 7
lines.note: Jerome says the surname Pamphili, which Eusebius bore, came from this friendship (Lives of Illustrious Men 81).

lines.text: He and Pamphilus write a Defense of Origen together, which he says they prepared carefully because of those who found fault with that earlier church teacher.
He gathers material from the library at Aelia, the Roman name for Jerusalem, where the letters of learned men had been kept.

He sets out his plan: the lines of bishops in the great churches, those who spoke or wrote the faith, those who led others into error, and those who stood firm under blood and torture down to his own day.
He says he is the first to enter on the subject and is traveling a lonely and untrodden path, finding only brief fragments left by those before him.
lines.note: This is his own claim. Sozomen, about a century later, names Clement, Hegesippus and Africanus among the writers who had set down the church's past before him (Sozomen I.1).

lines.text: He gathers the passages from older writers that he thinks fit his work, and says he will bring them together in one historical narrative.
He copies the letter of Polycrates of Ephesus to Victor and the church of Rome on the day for keeping Easter into his History in full.
He gives letters taken from the archives at Edessa, which he says were translated word for word from the Syriac.

timeline.headline: The persecution, seen and written down
timeline.witness: Eusebius, an eyewitness by his own account

lines.text: Imperial edicts order the churches leveled to the ground and the Scriptures burned, office holders degraded, and household servants who persist in Christianity deprived of freedom.
lines.note: Eusebius places this in the nineteenth year of Diocletian, in March. The Martyrs of Palestine gives April, and McGiffert's note reports that Lactantius, who was at Nicomedia, gives February 23.

lines.when: Not long after the first edict
lines.text: Further decrees order the rulers of the churches in every place thrown into prison and then forced by every means to sacrifice, to make an offering to the Roman gods.
He writes that he saw with his own eyes the houses of prayer thrown down, the Scriptures burned in the market squares, and the leaders of the churches hiding or caught and mocked by their enemies.
He sets himself a rule: he will not record those shaken by the persecution, only what may help his readers and those after them.
He says he was present at Tyre when martyrs were thrown to wild beasts, and that the beasts would not touch them.
lines.note: A wonder, told in his own voice.

lines.text: He says he was on the spot in the Thebais, in upper Egypt, and saw large crowds in one day, some beheaded and others tortured by fire, until the executioners grew weary.
His dearest friend Pamphilus is jailed and put to death with his companions, twelve in all.

timeline.headline: The council at Nicaea, and after

lines.text: Arius, in a letter, lists Eusebius of Caesarea among the bishops of the East who, he says, have been condemned for saying that God existed before his Son.
lines.reference: Arius to Eusebius of Nicomedia, in Theodoret, Church History I.4
lines.note: Arius's own claim, kept by Theodoret about a century later. Arius taught that the Son had a beginning.

lines.text: At the council of bishops at Nicaea, a paper of faith presented by Eusebius, his church's creed, is read before the emperor and declared good. He says he held this faith as he believed and taught it as a priest and as a bishop.
lines.reference: Eusebius, letter to his church, in McGiffert's Prolegomena
lines.note: The creed is the church's short statement of belief, said at baptism.

lines.text: The emperor advises all present to agree to the creed the bishops draw up and to sign it, with the single word homoousios added, which says the Son is of the same substance as the Father.
lines.reference: Eusebius, letter to his church, in McGiffert's Prolegomena

lines.text: Eusebius says they asked in what sense the words were meant, and questions and explanations followed. He assented, he writes, for the sake of peace and so as not to fall from the right belief.
lines.reference: Eusebius, letter to his church, in McGiffert's Prolegomena; Socrates I.8

lines.text: Socrates, about a century later, says he held aloof for a short time, then signed with the rest and sent his people a copy of the creed, so that no one might impugn his motives.
Athanasius, who was at the council and was his opponent, says he had refused the day before, then signed.
lines.reference: Athanasius, Defence of the Nicene Definition 3

lines.text: Eustathius, bishop of Antioch, accuses him of perverting the Nicene creed. Eusebius denies it and answers with a charge of his own.

After Eustathius is deposed, one party at Antioch asks for Eusebius to be moved there from Caesarea. He refuses the bishopric, and the emperor writes to praise him for keeping to the church's rule that a bishop stays with the church he first received.
lines.reference: Socrates I.24; Life of Constantine III.61

lines.text: Athanasius refuses to attend a council the emperor has called at Caesarea, fearing the artifices of Eusebius, bishop of that city, and of Eusebius of Nicomedia, Sozomen says.
lines.note: Sozomen wrote about a century later.

lines.text: The emperor calls many bishops to Tyre, first to settle the quarrels troubling the churches of Egypt and then to dedicate the church in Jerusalem.
lines.note: Eusebius's own telling blames a spirit of envy and names neither Athanasius nor Potamo.

lines.text: Epiphanius says Athanasius's opponents in Egypt charged him to the emperor with a broken cup used at the Lord's Supper, the church's meal of bread and wine, and with other crimes, and that the emperor, not knowing them to be slanderers, ordered a council at Tyre.
lines.note: Epiphanius wrote about forty years later, on Athanasius's side.

lines.text: Epiphanius says the emperor ordered Eusebius of Caesarea to judge, with some others, who he says leaned toward the Arians.
lines.note: The Arians were the followers of Arius, who taught that God's Son had a beginning.

lines.text: Potamo, a bishop from Egypt and a confessor, sees Eusebius seated as judge and Athanasius standing. He weeps, then cries out at Eusebius, asking how he got out of prison unless he promised the persecutors to do the forbidden thing, or did it.
lines.note: Potamo had lost an eye in the persecution. Only Epiphanius tells this.

lines.text: Eusebius rises in anger and breaks up the court. He says that if Athanasius's side come here and speak against him like this, their accusers must be telling the truth, for if they act as tyrants here they do so much more at home.
Socrates says Athanasius's accusers show a hand said to be that of Arsenius, and Athanasius brings Arsenius in alive with both hands, so that the charge fails.
Socrates says the council, on the report of a one-sided inquiry at Mareotis, by Alexandria, votes to depose Athanasius as bishop, and that its sentence says nothing of the failed charge of murder.
The bishops of Egypt, on Athanasius's side, write that Eusebius of Caesarea was accused by their confessors over a sacrifice.
lines.reference: Athanasius, Defence Against the Arians, letter of the council of Egypt
lines.note: The Greek has only over a sacrifice; the English translation adds to idols.

lines.text: Rufinus, writing later in Latin, tells a like scene at Tyre in which a confessor stops the bishop of Jerusalem from sitting in the council. He does not name Eusebius.
He gives several public orations at the dedication of the church in Jerusalem.

timeline.headline: The emperor he knew, and the Life of Constantine

lines.text: He sees Constantine as a young man, passing through Palestine at the right hand of the senior emperor.
The emperor himself, long afterwards and on oath, tells Eusebius of a sign in the sky, a cross of light above the sun.
lines.note: A wonder, told in the emperor's voice. Eusebius says it would be hard to believe from any other person.

lines.text: Eusebius is allowed to give a discourse on the Savior's tomb in the emperor's hearing. The emperor stands to listen and will not sit on the throne he is offered.
He writes the Life of Constantine, a book on the emperor's faith, and says he will pass over the wars and laws and speak only of the emperor's religious character.
lines.note: Socrates says the book is more intent on the emperor's praise than on an accurate account (Socrates I.1). Its telling of Tyre names neither Athanasius nor Potamo (IV.41).

lines.when: In the reign of Constantine's sons
lines.text: Eusebius dies. Acacius, his disciple, follows him as bishop of Caesarea and publishes a life of his master.

timeline.headline: Later writers: who began where he stopped, and how he was judged

lines.text: Socrates says Eusebius's History closed with the end of the persecution under Constantine, and begins his own history with what Eusebius left out.
Theodoret says he will begin his history from the period at which Eusebius's ends.
Sozomen counts Eusebius among the writers who had set down the church's past before him, and writes on from where they ended.

Rufinus, when the Goths broke into Italy, puts the Church History into Latin at the request of Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia. He says Eusebius's tenth book held little history and much praise of bishops, so he joins what history it had to the ninth and writes two books more himself.
Jerome puts Eusebius's Chronicle, a table of events by year, into Latin, and at Constantine's twentieth year notes that Eusebius writes the history up to there and that Jerome has added what follows.
Jerome says Eusebius's ten books of Church History were of the utmost assistance to his own book on Christian writers.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, preface

lines.text: In the late sixth century Evagrius names Eusebius first among four earlier church historians in the preface to his own history.
Athanasius says that in a letter to Euphration, Eusebius said plainly that Christ was not true God.
lines.reference: Athanasius, On the Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia 17

lines.text: Sabinus, who scorned the Council of Nicaea, still commends Eusebius as a trustworthy witness, Socrates says.
Socrates says that by not giving the reason for the troubles in Egypt after Nicaea, Eusebius has won the reputation of disingenuousness.
Socrates defends him against those who say he favored the views of Arius, since he was at Nicaea and agreed to what the council decided.
Philostorgius, as Photius's summary gives him, praises Eusebius but accuses him of erroneous opinions in matters of religion.
Jerome writes that Eusebius has composed a fine history of the Church and is the most open champion of the Arian impiety. In another work he calls him the standard-bearer of the Arian side.
lines.reference: Jerome, Letter 84; Apology against Rufinus I

lines.text: The Second Council of Nicaea, answering those who used Eusebius's letter to Constantia against holy images, has his letter to Euphration read.
lines.reference: Acts of the Second Council of Nicaea
lines.note: The Latin print of the acts is poor.
